title: What does Spring Kafka add over the raw Kafka client — `KafkaTemplate` (a thread-safe producer wrapper, `send(topic, key, value)` returning a `CompletableFuture`) for publishing, and `@KafkaListener` + listener containers for consuming — and how does the `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory` `concurrency` setting map listener threads to partitions (one consumer thread per partition, capped by partition count)?
shortTitle: What does Spring Kafka add over the raw client, and how does the listener container `concurrency` map threads to partitions?

s1_definition.profdef: Spring Kafka is an abstraction layer over the raw Apache Kafka client that removes boilerplate and integrates Kafka into the Spring programming model. For producing, `KafkaTemplate` is a thread-safe wrapper around a single shared `KafkaProducer` that exposes `send(topic, key, value)` returning a `CompletableFuture<SendResult>`. For consuming, `@KafkaListener` plus a listener container manages the poll loop, offset commits, threading, error handling, and lifecycle for you. The `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory` `concurrency` property spins up that many consumer threads in the same group, and Kafka's rebalance assigns partitions across them, so effective parallelism is capped by the number of partitions.
s1_definition.analogy: The raw Kafka client is like hiring a bank clerk and personally teaching them every step: open the counter, pull the next token, stamp it, close for the night, and clean up if they faint. Spring Kafka is like hiring through an agency that already trained the clerk — you just say what to do with each customer, and the agency handles opening, closing, rotating staff, and covering sick leave. At National Bank of India, `KafkaTemplate` is the one shared outgoing-mail clerk everyone uses, and `@KafkaListener` with `concurrency` is the agency assigning several clerks to several counters, one clerk per counter.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spring Kafka hides the poll loop and commit plumbing; `KafkaTemplate` is the thread-safe sender and `concurrency` gives you one consumer thread per partition up to the partition count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spring Kafka is an abstraction layer over the raw Apache Kafka client that removes boilerplate and integrates Kafka into the Spring programming model. For producing, `KafkaTemplate` is a thread-safe wrapper around a single shared `KafkaProducer` that exposes `send(topic, key, value)` returning a `CompletableFuture<SendResult>`. For consuming, `@KafkaListener` plus a listener container manages the poll loop, offset commits, threading, error handling, and lifecycle for you. The `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory` `concurrency` property spins up that many consumer threads in the same group, and Kafka's rebalance assigns partitions across them, so effective parallelism is capped by the number of partitions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The raw Kafka client is like hiring a bank clerk and personally teaching them every step: open the counter, pull the next token, stamp it, close for the night, and clean up if they faint. Spring Kafka is like hiring through an agency that already trained the clerk — you just say what to do with each customer, and the agency handles opening, closing, rotating staff, and covering sick leave. At National Bank of India, `KafkaTemplate` is the one shared outgoing-mail clerk everyone uses, and `@KafkaListener` with `concurrency` is the agency assigning several clerks to several counters, one clerk per counter.

**One line to remember:** Spring Kafka hides the poll loop and commit plumbing; `KafkaTemplate` is the thread-safe sender and `concurrency` gives you one consumer thread per partition up to the partition count.

sections.s2_technical:
With the raw client you must construct a `KafkaProducer`, call `producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>(...))`, deal with the returned `Future`, flush, and close it yourself, and you must not create one per request because producers are heavy. Spring Kafka gives you `KafkaTemplate`, which wraps one shared producer and is fully thread-safe, so every thread in the application can call it. The call looks like `kafkaTemplate.send("txn.events", "SAV2001", event)` and returns a `CompletableFuture<SendResult<String, TxnEvent>>`. You attach callbacks: `future.whenComplete((result, ex) -> { if (ex == null) log.info("sent to partition " + result.getRecordMetadata().partition()); else log.severe("send failed"); })`. This is non-blocking by default, and you only block with `future.get()` if you truly need synchronous confirmation.

On the consuming side, the raw client forces you to write an infinite `while (true)` loop that calls `poll`, iterates records, handles exceptions, commits offsets, and shuts down cleanly. Spring Kafka replaces all of that with a declarative `@KafkaListener(topics = "txn.events", groupId = "settlement")` on a method, and a listener container runs the poll loop for you behind the scenes. The container deserializes each record, invokes your method, commits offsets according to the configured acknowledgement mode, catches exceptions and routes them to an error handler, and manages start and stop with the Spring lifecycle. You write only the business logic: `public void onTxn(TxnEvent event) { settlementService.settle(event); }`.

The `concurrency` setting on `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory` controls parallelism. If you set `factory.setConcurrency(3)`, the container creates three child containers, each with its own consumer, all in the same consumer group. Kafka's group coordinator then runs a rebalance and distributes the topic's partitions across those three consumers. The crucial rule is that a single partition is only ever assigned to one consumer in the group at a time, so you can never have more useful consumer threads than partitions. If the topic has twelve partitions and you set concurrency to three, each thread owns four partitions; if the topic has two partitions and you set concurrency to three, one thread sits idle because there is no third partition to give it.

A few senior nuances matter here. First, ordering is preserved per partition, so if you key by account id, all of Rajesh's events land on the same partition and are processed in order by a single thread, even with high concurrency. Second, the concurrency number is the upper bound of threads in that one application instance; if you scale to multiple instances, the partitions are shared across all consumers in the group globally, so total parallelism is still capped by partition count across the whole group. Third, `KafkaTemplate` being one shared producer is intentional, because a Kafka producer batches and compresses across threads for throughput, so you should not create a template per request. The practical sizing rule I give juniors is to choose a partition count that matches your peak desired parallelism, then set concurrency per instance so that instances times concurrency does not exceed partitions.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem at National Bank of India is that the settlement team is drowning in producer and consumer boilerplate, and a single-threaded consumer cannot keep up with transaction volume.

Problem 1 — every service that publishes a transaction event writes the same twenty lines of raw producer setup, and some juniors accidentally create a new producer per request, which exhausts connections and kills throughput. This is exactly what `KafkaTemplate` solves: one shared, thread-safe sender that every part of the code reuses, with a clean `send` call that returns a future for the acknowledgement.

Problem 2 — the settlement consumer processes transactions one at a time on a single thread, so during a busy market open it falls hours behind. The team wants several threads consuming in parallel without writing their own thread pool and without breaking per-account ordering. This is exactly what `@KafkaListener` with `concurrency` solves: set concurrency to match the partition count, Kafka assigns partitions across the threads, and because events are keyed by account id, each account's events stay ordered on one partition and one thread.

The code will define a TxnEvent, a `TxnEventPublisher` that uses a simulated thread-safe template to send keyed events and log the resulting partition, and a `SettlementConsumer` whose method handles one event. A `ListenerContainerSimulator` will model the `concurrency` behaviour by assigning partitions to a fixed set of worker threads and showing that per-account ordering is preserved and that extra threads beyond the partition count stay idle. The demo step is: publish events for Rajesh and Priya across four partitions, configure concurrency of two and then five, and observe the thread-to-partition mapping and the idle thread.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway migration)
CREATE TABLE settlements (
    txn_id     VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    partition  INT NOT NULL,
    worker     VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    settled_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      acks: all
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
    listener:
      # concurrency = number of consumer threads in this instance
      concurrency: 4
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four transaction events, two keyed by SAV2001 for Rajesh and two keyed by CUR3001 for Priya, published to a topic with four partitions.

Step 1: The publisher, modelling `KafkaTemplate`, takes TXN-1 with key SAV2001. It computes the partition the same way Kafka does, by hashing the key and taking it modulo the partition count, and sends it. The send returns a future and logs the destination partition when the acknowledgement arrives.

Step 2: TXN-2, also keyed SAV2001, hashes to the same partition as TXN-1. This is the key guarantee: both of Rajesh's events land on the same partition, so their order is preserved end to end.

Step 3: TXN-3 and TXN-4, keyed CUR3001, hash to Priya's partition, again both on the same one, keeping her events ordered.

Step 4: Now the consumer side. With concurrency set to two over four partitions, the container simulator creates two threads and spreads the four partitions across them, so each thread owns two partitions. No partition is shared, and ordering within each partition stays on one thread.

Step 5: With concurrency set to five over four partitions, the simulator creates five threads but there are only four partitions to hand out, so four threads each own one partition and the fifth thread sits idle, demonstrating the hard cap at partition count.

Step 6: The output shows the keyed sends with their partitions, then the two assignment scenarios, including the idle thread warning.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Business code (many threads)
    │ kafkaTemplate.send("txn.events", accountId, event)
    ▼
  KafkaTemplate (ONE shared thread-safe producer)
    │ partition = hash(key) % 4
    ▼
  ┌──────────── topic: txn.events (4 partitions) ────────────┐
  │ P0        P1 (SAV2001)   P2        P3 (CUR3001)           │
  └──────┬───────────┬───────────┬───────────┬───────────────┘
         │           │           │           │
   concurrency=2 → rebalance assigns partitions to threads
         ▼           ▼           ▼           ▼
  thread-0 owns [P0,P2]        thread-1 owns [P1,P3]
    │ @KafkaListener method      │ @KafkaListener method
    ▼                            ▼
  SettlementConsumer.onTxn(event)   (per-partition order preserved)

  concurrency=5 → thread-4 IDLE (only 4 partitions exist)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Spring Kafka Producer + Listener Container ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Template Method: KafkaTemplate wraps the fixed send/flush steps    │
  │   WHY: callers provide topic/key/value, plumbing is standardised  │
  │ Observer Pattern: listener container pushes records to @KafkaListener│
  │   WHY: business code reacts; the poll loop is inverted into callbacks│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Publisher only sends; Consumer only handles one event          │
  │ O: raise concurrency or partitions, no change to business method  │
  │ D: business code depends on KafkaTemplate, not raw KafkaProducer   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ TxnEventPublisher        │     │ ListenerContainerSimulator    │
  │ ─────────────────────────│     │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ - partitionCount: int    │     │ - concurrency: int            │
  │ ─────────────────────────│     │ - partitionCount: int         │
  │ + send(topic,key,event)  │     │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │   : CompletableFuture    │     │ + assign(): void              │
  └───────────┬──────────────┘     └───────────────────────────────┘
              │ sends
              ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ TxnEvent (+txnId +accountId +amount)       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a consumer thread in the group ──────────────────

  [CREATED] ──join group──→ [ASSIGNED partitions] ──poll/handle──→ [ACTIVE]
      │                          │
      │ no partition left         │ rebalance (instance added/removed)
      ▼                          ▼
  [IDLE]                     [REASSIGNED]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────────

  1. publisher.send("txn.events", "SAV2001", TXN-1)
  2.   → partition = hash("SAV2001") % 4 = 1
  3.   → future completes → log partition=1
  4. simulator(concurrency=2).assign()
  5.   → thread-0 = [P0,P2], thread-1 = [P1,P3]
  6. simulator(concurrency=5).assign()
  7.   → thread-4 IDLE (cap reached)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring Kafka is a thin, productive abstraction over the raw Apache Kafka client that fits Kafka into the Spring programming model and removes the repetitive plumbing. On the producing side, `KafkaTemplate` wraps a single shared, thread-safe producer, and you publish with `send(topic, key, value)`, which returns a CompletableFuture carrying the send result so you can attach success and failure callbacks without blocking. The important discipline is that this is one shared producer reused across every thread, because a Kafka producer batches and compresses across threads for throughput, so you never create one per request.

On the consuming side, instead of hand-writing an infinite poll loop with manual deserialization, offset commits, error handling, and shutdown, you annotate a method with `@KafkaListener` and a listener container runs that loop for you. It deserializes each record, calls your method, commits offsets based on the configured acknowledgement mode, routes exceptions to an error handler, and starts and stops with the Spring lifecycle, so you write only the business logic.

Parallelism comes from the `concurrency` setting on the `ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory`. Setting concurrency to a number creates that many consumer threads in the same group, and Kafka's rebalance distributes the topic's partitions across them. The rule I always state is that a partition is owned by exactly one consumer in the group at a time, so you can never have more useful consumer threads than partitions; if concurrency exceeds the partition count, the extra threads sit idle.

In the settlement service I built at National Bank of India, I keyed every transaction event by account id, so all of Rajesh's events landed on one partition and stayed strictly ordered even under high concurrency. I matched the partition count to the parallelism we wanted and set concurrency per instance so that instances times concurrency never exceeded the partition count. The nuance I add for an interviewer is that scaling across multiple instances still shares the same partitions within the consumer group, so the hard cap on parallelism is always the partition count across the whole group, which is why choosing the partition count up front is the real capacity-planning decision.
